concept.name: P-value
concept.definition: In null-hypothesis significance testing, the probability - computed assuming the null hypothesis is true - of obtaining a test statistic at least as extreme as the one actually observed. The smaller the p-value, the more incompatible the data are with the null model.
concept.intuition: It answers: 'If there were really no effect, how often would luck alone produce a result this strong?' A p-value of 0.01 means only 1% of no-effect worlds give data this extreme.
concept.mechanics: Specify H0, a test statistic, and whether the test is one- or two-tailed; then compute the tail probability of the observed statistic under the null sampling distribution. H0 is rejected at significance level alpha when p <= alpha; the 0.05 convention traces to Fisher (1925).
concept.formula: p = P(T >= t_obs | H0) for a right-tailed test (analogously for left- or two-tailed tests), where T is the test statistic and t_obs its observed value.
concept.failure_modes: P-values shrink with sample size regardless of economic importance, so a trivially small edge becomes 'significant' with enough trades. They are invalidated by data snooping, optional stopping, and multiple testing (testing many signals guarantees small p-values by chance), and they assume the null model, including its distribution, is correctly specified.
concept.misconceptions: A p-value is NOT the probability that the null hypothesis is true, nor the probability the result arose by chance alone; and p > 0.05 is not evidence of no effect (absence of evidence). The ASA's 2016 statement stresses that p-values measure neither effect size nor the importance of a result.
concept.example: A fair coin lands heads 14 times in 20 flips; the two-tailed p-value under H0: p = 0.5 is 0.115, above 0.05, so fairness is not rejected - one more head (15/20) would give p = 0.041 and a rejection.

citations.source: Wikipedia, 'P-value' (citing Wasserstein & Lazar 2016, 'The ASA's Statement on p-Values', The American Statistician 70(2))
